summary: Provides protocol identifier examples that can be used to produce valid protocolDirTable INDEX encodings defined by the RMON MIB and the RMON Protocol Identifier Reference. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Network monitors count how much traffic each kind of protocol carries, and they keep those counts in a table where every protocol has a row. This memo is a catalogue of label forms for those rows, so that two monitors name the same traffic the same way. It is a convenience list rather than a standard: the rules for writing the labels are in RFC 2895.

questions: what is rmon protocol identifier macro
how are rmon protocol ids encoded
subtitle: Worked examples that show how an RMON-2 agent names each protocol encapsulation, so two monitors count the same traffic the same way.

tldr.problem: An RMON-2 agent records how much traffic each protocol carries, and two agents must name the same protocol the same way or their numbers cannot be compared.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER macros for well-known protocol stacks. Each macro states which values in the traffic select a protocol inside its parent, and how those values are written as bytes in the protocolDirTable index.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational, not a standard: an agent can conform to the RMON-2 MIB without it. The working group stopped maintaining the repository, so the encoding rules now live only in RFC 2895.

today: RFC 2896 is an Informational memo and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. The memo itself says the RMONMIB working group stopped maintaining it because the RMON vendor community stopped contributing. The encoding rules it refers to are in RFC 2895.

sections.title: What the Memo Contains
sections.content:
This memo is a collection of examples. It gives a PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER macro for a number of well-known protocols, and each macro can be turned into a valid INDEX value for the protocolDirTable of the RMON-2 Management Information Base, using the mapping rules defined in RFC 2895.

The memo is explicit that it is not a standard. A conformant implementation of the RMON-2 MIB can be built without these protocol identifiers, and the memo says it does not specify any IETF standard. It is published to encourage better interoperability between RMON-2 agent implementations by putting a great deal of protocol information in one document.

This is the second revision of the RMON Protocol Identifiers document. The first, RFC 2074, was split in two: the standards-track Reference portion became RFC 2895, and this memo holds the non-normative portion. It is intended to replace Section 5 of RFC 2074.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a list of label forms for the RMON-2 protocol directory table, the table where a monitor records how much traffic each protocol carries. Each form says which values in the traffic pick out a protocol and how those values are written down as bytes. It is a convenience list, not a standard.

sections.title: How It Fits With the RMON Documents
sections.content:
The memo opens with a summary of the SNMP Management Framework, which has five parts: an overall architecture (RFC 2571); the Structure of Management Information, which is how managed objects are described and named, in its first version (RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215) and its second version, SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580); the message protocols SNMPv1 (RFC 1157), SNMPv2c (RFC 1901 and RFC 1906) and SNMPv3 (RFC 2572 and RFC 2574); the protocol operations for accessing management information (RFC 1905); and a set of fundamental applications (RFC 2573) with the view-based access control mechanism (RFC 2575).

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base, or MIB. The memo defines no MIB module of its own.

The RMON-2 MIB (RFC 2021) uses hierarchically formatted OCTET STRINGs to identify individual protocol encapsulations in the protocolDirTable. The syntax of that protocol identifier descriptor is defined in RFC 2895. This memo is meant to be used with RFC 2895 and with that table only: it says it is not relevant to any other MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: RMON-2 builds on SNMP, the protocol computers use to ask devices about themselves. The memo places its examples in that setting and explains that the table it supports is used by no other management database.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Protocol Identifier Macro
sections.content:
The macros build on base layer identifiers, which the memo takes from Section 4 of RFC 2895: ether2, llc, snap, vsnap, ianaAssigned and 802-1Q. A network layer protocol identifier macro follows its base layer identifier immediately and adds information about the network layer.

Every macro has PARAMETERS and ATTRIBUTES clauses. At the network layer the supported parameters are countsFragments(0) and tracksSessions(1), and the supported attributes are hasChildren(0) and addressRecognitionCapable(1). An agent may implement a subset of either. The attributes it supports also decide which tables the protocol can appear in, for example the protocol distribution, host and matrix tables.

The other clauses describe how one protocol nests inside another. CHILDREN says which value in the traffic selects the child and how that value is encoded as bytes. ADDRESS-FORMAT describes the addresses used at that layer. DECODING gives worked INDEX values. The list after ::= says which parent identifiers the protocol attaches to, and the protocol name is used for the ProtocolDirDescr field.

The memo says the list is not exhaustive. Any protocol that can encapsulate other protocols must be documented so that its children can be encoded into protocolDirID strings, but a leaf protocol can be identified by an implementation even if it is not listed, as long as its parent is documented.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol gets a short form with fixed parts: the parameters and attributes the monitor supports, how a child protocol is picked out of its parent, the address format, and the list of parents it can sit under. Filling in the form produces the bytes that name the protocol in the table.

sections.title: The TCP/IP Stack
sections.content:
Section 3.1.1 is the bulk of the memo: the TCP/IP stack. It starts with arp, whose Address Resolution Protocol messages are counted separately from Reverse ARP packets, and then ip, the Internet Protocol.

Children of ip are selected by the value in the one-octet Protocol field of the IP header and are encoded as [ 0.0.0.a ], where a is that field value. The fragment 0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.1 therefore names the encapsulation ether2.ip.icmp. Children of tcp and udp are selected by the 16-bit source or destination port and are encoded as [ 0.0.a.b ], with both bytes in network byte order. The fragment 0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.6.0.0.0.23 names ether2.ip.tcp.telnet, and 0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.17.0.0.0.161 names ether2.ip.udp.snmp.

IP can be encapsulated within itself, so the memo notes that ether2.ip.ipip4.udp and ether2.ip.udp are different entries in the table and the agent assigns two different local protocol index values to them. The ip macro lists the values it attaches to: 0x0800 for ether2, snap and 802-1Q, 0x06 for llc, and 0x02000006 for 802.1Q LLC.
sections.plainLanguage: For TCP/IP, the Protocol field in the IP header picks the protocol inside IP, and the port number picks the protocol inside TCP or UDP. Those values are written into the label as bytes, so the fragment 0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.6.0.0.0.23 stands for IP over TCP carrying telnet.

sections.title: Other Protocol Stacks and Multi-Stack Use
sections.content:
The memo then gives macros for other protocol families, each under its own heading: the Novell IPX stack, the XEROX stack, the AppleTalk stack, the Banyon Vines stack, the DECNet stack, the IBM SNA stack and the NetBEUI/NetBIOS family. Children of IPX are selected by the 8-bit packet type field and encoded as [ 0.0.0.a ], and the IPX address format is 4 bytes of network number followed by 6 bytes of host address. Children of NetBIOS and NetBEUI are identified by a 32-bit enumeration encoded as [ a.b.c.d ].

Section 3.2 covers multi-stack protocols, which run over more than one transport. smb, the Microsoft Server Message Block protocol, is a child of the NetBEUI family. notes, the Lotus Notes protocol, appears both under NetBEUI and over TCP and UDP port 1352. ccmail, the Lotus CC Mail protocol, appears over TCP and UDP port 3264. snmp covers the SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 protocol versions over UDP port 161 and TCP port 161, and snmptrap uses UDP port 162 and TCP port 162.

The memo says some of these protocols may no longer be in use. They are included so that an agent which meets such traffic can describe it in the same way another agent would.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo also gives forms for older network protocol families, and for applications that run over more than one transport, so a monitor labels them the same way as anyone else.

sections.title: Security and Maintenance Status
sections.content:
The security section says the memo contains textual descriptions of well-known networking protocols, not the definition of any networking behavior, so no security considerations are raised by its publication.

On maintenance, the RMONMIB working group decided to discontinue upkeep of this Protocol Identifier Macro repository document because of a lack of contributions from the RMON vendor community. The memo is published as an aid in implementing the protocolDirTable.

The separation from the Reference document is deliberate. It allows frequent updates to the examples without republishing any MIB objects or protocolDirTable INDEX encoding rules. The base layer and IANA assigned protocol identifier macros stay in RFC 2895, because those encoding values are defined by the RMONMIB working group.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says it defines no network behaviour, so it raises no security questions of its own. The working group that kept the list stopped updating it because vendors stopped sending new entries.

viz.caption: THE ip MACRO AS PRINTED IN THE RFC

data.title: ip PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER
data.code:
ip PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER
    PARAMETERS {
       countsFragments(0)  -- This parameter applies to all child
                           -- protocols.
    }
    ATTRIBUTES {
     hasChildren(0),
     addressRecognitionCapable(1)
    }
    DESCRIPTION
       "The protocol identifiers for the Internet Protocol (IP). Note
       that IP may be encapsulated within itself, so more than one of
       the following identifiers may be present in a particular
       protocolDirID string."
    CHILDREN
       "Children of 'ip' are selected by the value in the Protocol field
       (one octet), as defined in the PROTOCOL NUMBERS table within the
       Assigned Numbers Document.

       The value of the Protocol field is encoded in an octet string as
       [ 0.0.0.a ], where 'a' is the protocol field .

       Children of 'ip' are encoded as [ 0.0.0.a ], and named as 'ip a'
       where 'a' is the protocol field value.  For example, a
       protocolDirID-fragment value of:
          0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.1

       defines an encapsulation of ICMP (ether2.ip.icmp)"
    ::= {
       ether2     0x0800,
       llc        0x06,
       snap       0x0800,
       -- ip         4,           ** represented by the ipip4 macro
       -- ip         94,          ** represented by the ipip macro
       802-1Q     0x0800,         -- [0.0.8.0]
       802-1Q     0x02000006      -- 1Q-LLC [2.0.0.6]
    }
